title: What training does Title IX require for coordinators, investigators and decision-makers?
description: Which Title IX rule is in force as at November 2026, who 34 CFR 106.45(b)(1)(iii) requires to be trained, on what, and the seven year training record duty.
shortAnswer: Under the US Department of Education's Title IX regulations at 34 CFR 106.45(b)(1)(iii), schools and colleges receiving federal funds must train their Title IX Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers and informal resolution facilitators on the definition of sexual harassment, the scope of their program, how to run the grievance process, and how to serve impartially. The 2020 rule is the version in force as at November 2026, and training materials must be kept for seven years and posted online.
keyTakeaways: The 2020 Title IX Rule (85 FR 30026, effective August 14, 2020) is the rule in force. The 2024 Rule was vacated in full on January 9, 2025, and the Department recodified the pre-2024 text in a final rule effective September 29, 2026.
Section 106.45(b)(1)(iii) names four trained roles: Title IX Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and anyone who facilitates an informal resolution process.
Decision-makers need added training on live hearing technology and relevance, and investigators need training on relevance for the investigative report.
All training materials must be kept for seven years and published on the institution's website, or made available for public inspection if it has no website (34 CFR 106.45(b)(10)).
The in-force rule sets no training frequency and no all-employee training mandate. The vacated 2024 Rule had required annual training for all employees.
regulator: Office for Civil Rights (OCR), US Department of Education
appliesTo: Recipients of federal financial assistance from the US Department of Education that operate an education program or activity, including school districts, public and private colleges and universities
Title IX Coordinators designated under 34 CFR 106.8(a)
Investigators, decision-makers (including appeal decision-makers) and informal resolution facilitators
Advisors provided by a postsecondary institution for live hearings, where the institution chooses to train them

sections.heading: Which Title IX rule is in force as at November 2026?

blocks.text: The 2020 Title IX Rule is in force, and since September 29, 2026 its text is again printed in the Code of Federal Regulations. The Department of Education published the 2020 Rule on May 19, 2020, and it took effect on August 14, 2020. A replacement rule published on April 29, 2024 (89 FR 33474) was enjoined in 26 states during 2024 and then vacated in full.

According to the Department's [Recodification of Title IX Rules](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/29/2026-19929/recodification-of-title-ix-rules) final rule (91 FR 61308), the 2024 Rule was vacated in final judgments in Tennessee v. Cardona (E.D. Ky., January 9, 2025) and Carroll Independent School District v. Department of Education (N.D. Tex., February 19, 2025). The Department announced on January 31, 2025 that it would enforce the pre-2024 regulations, and a Dear Colleague Letter of February 4, 2025 from the Office for Civil Rights stated that it would enforce Title IX under the 2020 Rule. The recodification rule took effect on September 29, 2026.

blocks.title: One sentence was not restored
blocks.text: The recodified text omits a single sentence of the 2020 version of 106.45(b)(6)(i) that barred decision-makers from relying on statements by a party or witness who did not submit to cross-examination. A federal court vacated that sentence in Victim Rights Law Center v. Cardona (D. Mass. 2021). Hearing training written between 2020 and 2021 may still teach the old exclusion rule and should be checked.

For training owners the practical consequence is simple: content built for the 2024 Rule, such as all-employee modules and its sex-based harassment definitions, does not reflect the regulation now in force. Programs revised in 2024 should be reviewed against the current text, using the method in [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

sections.heading: Who must be trained under 34 CFR 106.45?

blocks.text: Four roles must be trained: Title IX Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and any person who facilitates an informal resolution process. [34 CFR 106.45(b)(1)(iii)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-34/section-106.45) first requires that none of these people has "a conflict of interest or bias for or against complainants or respondents generally or an individual complainant or respondent", and then sets the training duty.

Every recipient must have at least one such Coordinator. [34 CFR 106.8(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-34/section-106.8) requires each recipient to "designate and authorize at least one employee" as the Title IX Coordinator and to notify applicants, students, parents of elementary and secondary students, employees and unions of the Coordinator's name or title, office address, email address and telephone number. Section 106.8(b)(2) requires that contact information and the nondiscrimination policy to be prominently displayed on the recipient's website and in each handbook or catalog.

Decision-makers include whoever determines responsibility and whoever decides an appeal. Under 106.45(b)(7)(i) the decision-maker cannot be the Title IX Coordinator or the investigator, so most institutions need a trained pool large enough to separate those roles and to cover conflicts.

sections.heading: What must Title IX training cover?

blocks.text: The regulation lists the required topics directly. All four roles must be trained on "the definition of sexual harassment in § 106.30, the scope of the recipient's education program or activity, how to conduct an investigation and grievance process including hearings, appeals, and informal resolution processes, as applicable, and how to serve impartially, including by avoiding prejudgment of the facts at issue, conflicts of interest, and bias".

blocks.text: The same paragraph controls the content of the materials themselves. Any materials used to train these roles "must not rely on sex stereotypes and must promote impartial investigations and adjudications of formal complaints of sexual harassment". That standard applies to slides, scenarios and assessment questions alike, which makes item review part of compliance rather than a quality nicety.

sections.heading: How does training differ for K-12 schools and colleges?

blocks.text: Colleges must hold live hearings, so their decision-makers need hearing technology and live relevance training, while K-12 schools may decide without a hearing. Under 106.45(b)(6)(i), a postsecondary grievance process "must provide for a live hearing" with cross-examination by each party's advisor, and the decision-maker must rule on the relevance of each question before it is answered and explain any exclusion.

Under 106.45(b)(6)(ii), elementary and secondary schools "may, but need not, provide for a hearing", but the decision-maker must still let each party submit written, relevant questions and limited follow-up questions. K-12 decision-makers therefore still need relevance training, applied to written questions.

Notice duties also differ. The definition of actual knowledge in [34 CFR 106.30](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-34/section-106.30) includes notice to "any employee of an elementary and secondary school", so in K-12 any employee's knowledge can trigger the school's response obligations. In postsecondary institutions, notice must reach the Coordinator or an official with authority to institute corrective measures, and the definition states that having been trained to report "does not qualify an individual" as such an official.

sections.heading: What training records must be kept and published?

blocks.text: Recipients must keep all Title IX training materials for seven years and publish them. Under 34 CFR 106.45(b)(10)(i)(D), a recipient must maintain for seven years "all materials used to train Title IX Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and any person who facilitates an informal resolution process", and "must make these training materials publicly available on its website", or make them available on request for public inspection if it has no website.

items: Keep every version of each training deck, video, handout and scenario, dated, for seven years from use. Overwriting a slide deck in place destroys the record.
Publish the current materials on the Title IX web page. Third party training is covered too, so licensing terms must allow publication.
Keep attendance or completion records that tie each trained person to the material version they received, so an investigator's training can be shown at the date of a specific case.
Record conflict of interest and bias checks for each case alongside the training record, since 106.45(b)(1)(iii) treats both as one requirement.
Keep the seven year case records required by 106.45(b)(10)(i)(A) to (C) linked to the trained personnel who handled them.

blocks.text: Seven years is longer than many default learning system retention settings. The considerations in [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records) and [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) apply directly.

sections.heading: How often must Title IX training happen, and do all employees need it?

blocks.text: The rule in force sets no frequency and does not require training for all employees. Section 106.45(b)(1)(iii) requires that the named roles "receive training" but does not say how often. Institutions must decide when training is refreshed, which normally means before a person first handles a case and again when the policy, the hearing technology or the case law changes.

The vacated 2024 Rule took a different approach. Its 106.8(d) required training "promptly upon hiring or change of position" and "annually thereafter", and extended training to all employees. That provision is no longer in the CFR, but institutions may keep annual and all-staff training as policy choices. State laws can also impose their own training duties, as described for workplace harassment in [California and New York harassment training](/regulations/california-and-new-york-harassment-training).

Postsecondary institutions should not set Title IX refresh cycles in isolation. Officials who conduct disciplinary proceedings for dating violence, domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking must receive annual training under the Clery Act regulations, covered in [Clery Act training requirements](/regulations/clery-act-training-requirements). Many of those officials are also Title IX decision-makers, so one annual cycle often satisfies both, as set out in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: How can an institution map Title IX duties to evidence?

blocks.text: Map each regulatory sentence to a role, a timing rule and the record OCR would expect to see. The table below is an illustrative starting point for a postsecondary institution; a K-12 district would adjust the hearing rows.

blocks.text: Completion alone does not show that a decision-maker can apply the relevance rules under pressure. Scenario based assessment, discussed in [completion tracking vs competency verification](/compare/completion-tracking-vs-competency-verification), is the stronger evidence. Institutions building this into a wider program can follow [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations); sector context is on the [higher education](/industries/higher-education) page.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each sentence of 106.45(b)(1)(iii) to the role it applies to and the assessment point that evidences it, before any training material is written. When the regulation changes, as it did in 2020, 2024 and 2026, the map shows which lessons and questions are affected and keeps dated versions for the seven year retention period.

faqs.q: Is the 2024 Title IX rule enforceable anywhere?
faqs.a: No. The Department of Education states that the 2024 Rule was vacated in full by final judgments on January 9, 2025 and February 19, 2025, that it has not enforced the 2024 Rule since, and it repealed the 2024 Rule in a recodification final rule effective September 29, 2026. The 2020 Rule text is now the text in the CFR.

faqs.q: Do Title IX training materials really have to be public?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 106.45(b)(10)(i)(D) requires a recipient to make the materials used to train Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers and informal resolution facilitators publicly available on its website. A recipient without a website must make them available on request for public inspection. This applies to externally purchased training as well as in-house materials.

faqs.q: Does Title IX require a specific number of training hours?
faqs.a: No. The 2020 Rule specifies topics, roles and record keeping but no hours, format or frequency. The institution decides how long training runs and how often it repeats, and should be able to explain how its approach covers every topic listed in 106.45(b)(1)(iii).

faqs.q: Must advisors at college hearings be trained?
faqs.a: The rule does not list advisors among the roles that must be trained. A postsecondary institution must provide an advisor, without fee, to a party who has none at a live hearing, and that advisor conducts cross-examination. Many institutions train the advisors they appoint, but that is a policy choice rather than a requirement of 106.45(b)(1)(iii).
